entities.summary:
**Identity & Significance**: The Southern Ocean is the fifth-largest of the world's five oceans, covering an area of approximately 20.3 million square kilometers. It surrounds Antarctica and extends north to the coast of South America, Africa, and Australia, playing a crucial role in global climate regulation by driving ocean currents and influencing regional weather patterns.

**What Happened**: The Southern Ocean was formally designated as a separate ocean in 2000, after being recognized as a distinct body of water since the 1920s. Its discovery is attributed to British navigator Edward Bransfield, who sighted it on January 30, 1820, while working for the British Royal Navy.

**Legacy & Consequence**: The Southern Ocean's unique circulation patterns and marine life support some of the world's most biodiverse ecosystems, including the Antarctic Peninsula and surrounding islands. Its discovery has also led to a greater understanding of global climate change, as changes in ocean currents can have significant impacts on regional weather patterns.

**Vivid Closing Statistic**: The Southern Ocean is home to approximately 20% of the world's marine life, despite covering only about 5% of the Earth's surface.
